tier_reason: documentation/paper/Results.tex (first-party student report, not peer reviewed) gives boxplot medians for oxtra (a/b/c), QEMU 4.1.0 and native on primes and gzip; the repo holds only the gzip input files (documentation/paper/benchmarking/*.txt), no benchmark scripts, and timings ran inside system-mode QEMU on an unstated host CPU with host compiler flags unstated, so not A or B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper text: oxtra is 'up to twice as fast as QEMU' for small inputs. Medians, oxtra (c) vs QEMU 4.1.0: primes below 10,000 20.68 ms vs 54.71 ms (2.65x, derived from page data); gzip 132 kB 60.42 ms vs 154.83 ms (2.56x, derived from page data); gzip 526 kB 270.5 ms vs 348.9 ms (paper: 'merely 25% faster'); gzip 13 MB 2623 ms vs 3137 ms (paper: 20% faster); primes below 1,000,000 3685 ms vs 2720 ms (oxtra 35% slower). QEMU executes 1.70x (primes 10k) down to 1.13x (gzip 13 MB) as many RISC-V instructions as oxtra (c); oxtra (c) uses 3.87x (primes) and 2.55x (gzip) less peak memory than QEMU.
corrections.caveats: Student project report (documentation/paper/Paper.pdf, Results.tex), not peer reviewed. All timings were taken inside system-mode QEMU running Fedora RISC-V on an unstated host, which the authors say obscures the timing results; the large cases use only 5 runs. The README claims the current version 'consistently beats qemu in our toy examples', but the paper shows oxtra 35% slower on primes below 1 million and its advantage shrinking as inputs grow (the authors: 'oxtra quickly becomes slower than QEMU as input become larger'). The repo ships only the gzip input files, no benchmark scripts. Baseline is QEMU 4.1.0 (2019). oxtra supports only a small x86-64 subset, no SSE, statically linked musl binaries only (guests built with the project's musl-gcc fork). Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.

notes: Record accurate; numbers match Results.tex. Shortcomings: student report, emulated timings on unstated host, no benchmark scripts, loses 35% to QEMU on the larger primes run despite the README's 'consistently beats qemu', toy-scale x86 subset, abandoned since 2020.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A: the peer-reviewed OOPSLA 2021 paper (PDF reached via the author's fredrikbk.github.io repo) names PochiVM as the system measured, states the CPU (Intel i7-7700HQ), compiler and flags (Clang++ 10 -O3 -DNDEBUG, LLVM 10.0.0), and the public harness is in the repo (test_mini_db_backend_unit_test.cpp PaperBenchmark.TpchQuery1/3/5/6/10/12/14/19 and test_paper_microbenchmarks.cpp, both timing copy-and-patch against LLVM -O0..-O3 and the interpreter). The debug-build cap does not apply: the metric is code-generation time, where LLVM -O0 is LLVM's fastest mode, and the paper also reports the -O1..-O3 comparison.

corrections.claimed_speedup: OOPSLA 2021 paper, Section 7.3 and Fig. 24: on 8 TPC-H queries copy-and-patch generates code two orders of magnitude faster than LLVM -O0 (up to 276x) and three orders of magnitude faster than -O1/-O2/-O3 (1083x-1435x, average 1286x); the generated code runs on average 14% faster than LLVM -O0 but 22% slower than -O1, 25% slower than -O2 and 24% slower than -O3; the AST interpreter executes 6x-27x slower than copy-and-patch (Fig. 25). Example: TPC-H Q5 code generation takes 178 us versus 0.25 s with LLVM -O3, whose code is 1.2% faster.
corrections.baseline: LLVM 10.0.0 JIT backend of the same metaprogramming system at -O0 (also -O1/-O2/-O3) for code-generation time and generated-code speed, plus an in-house AST interpreter (about 1.5x faster than the Peloton interpreter)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Stencils and copy-and-patch runtime compiled by Clang++ 10 with -O3 -DNDEBUG; LLVM backend uses the LLVM 10.0.0 library (paper Section 7.1); repo CMakeLists.txt production flavor: clang++ -O3 -DNDEBUG -pthread
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-7700HQ at 2.80 GHz, single socket, 8 logical cores, turbo boost on, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 (paper Section 6.1, reused in 7.1)
corrections.workload: Eight TPC-H queries (Q1, Q3, Q5, Q6, Q10, Q12, Q14, Q19) with hand-coded query plans over a dbgen scale-factor-0.3 database (about 380 MB), lowered through PochiVM's C-like DSL to copy-and-patch, LLVM -O0..-O3 or an AST interpreter; plus Fibonacci, Euler sieve and quicksort microbenchmarks. Harness: test_mini_db_backend_unit_test.cpp (PaperBenchmark.TpchQuery*) and test_paper_microbenchmarks.cpp; each configuration repeated at least 100 times, average reported.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from the authors' peer-reviewed OOPSLA 2021 paper (Xu and Kjolstad, 'Copy-and-Patch Compilation'), not an independent run; the README itself has no numbers. Generated code beats only LLVM -O0 and is 22%-25% slower than -O1..-O3; the win is compile latency. The query compiler is a 600-line prototype with hand-coded plans for only 8 TPC-H queries (no SQL parser or planner). The stencil library takes 14 minutes on 6 threads to build at install time and uses 17.5 MB at runtime. The repo has no LICENSE file; the Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception grant is stated only in the README, alongside a non-binding request not to use it for harmful projects. Abandoned research prototype (last commit 2021-09-09, a July 2021 commit adds a FIXME for a known, unfixed bug). The WebAssembly numbers in the same paper belong to WasmNow (already catalogued). Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.

notes: Paper PDF reached at raw.githubusercontent.com/fredrikbk/fredrikbk.github.io/master/publications/copy-and-patch.pdf (also usable for a WasmNow retier: same paper, same i7-7700HQ). Record upgraded C to A with full methodology. Shortcomings: generated code slower than LLVM -O1+, prototype query compiler with 8 hand-planned TPC-H queries, no LICENSE file (README grant only), abandoned since 2021.

tier_reason: README Performance section gives first-party Google Benchmark output against native C++ with only 'a CPU that supports AVX2' and '-O2'; no CPU model or compiler version, and the printed benchmark names (BM_rapidudf_vector_expr_func, BM_native_wilson_ctr, BM_rapidudf_fib_func) are not in the current harness rapidudf/tests/benchmark.cc, which was rewritten, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: trigonometric expression over a 4099-element double array, vectorised JIT 33,962 ns vs native 207,145 ns and scalar JIT 207,713 ns ('reaching 6.09'; 6.10x vs native, derived from page data); Wilson CTR over floats, vectorised JIT 6,661 ns vs native 69,961 ns ('reaching 10.5'). Scalar JIT fib: 22,547 ns vs 38,933 ns for native built at -O0 (debug baseline), but 22,557 ns vs 19,246 ns for native at GCC -O2, i.e. the JIT is 17% slower than native -O2 (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: README: optimisation flag -O2 for the vectorised tests; native fib built at GCC -O0 and -O2; JIT at RapidUDF's default LLVM optimize_level 2 (LLVM 18+); compiler version and -march not stated. Current harness rapidudf/tests/BUILD builds benchmark.cc with copts -O2.
corrections.caveats: The 6x and 10.5x wins come from SIMD vectorisation (Highway, AVX2) against a scalar native loop that GCC cannot auto-vectorise at -O2 because of libm calls; scalar JIT is 17% slower than native -O2 on fib, and the only 'faster than native' scalar result is against a -O0 build. In the current code sin, cos and log10 on vectors use Highway contrib math (hn::Sin, hn::Cos, hn::Log10, a few ULP and range-limited) rather than glibc libm, with SLEEF only for cosh, tan, erf, pow and similar, so results are not bit-identical to the native baseline. The README numbers come from an older harness: their benchmark names do not appear in the current rapidudf/tests/benchmark.cc, which now runs scalar/vector x native/JIT for trig, Wilson CTR f32/f64, an order rule and fib(20). CPU model and compiler version unstated. Baseline is native C++, not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.

notes: Record accurate apart from the fib wording (JIT 17% slower than native -O2, not on par). Shortcomings: win is SIMD math versus scalar libm, not JIT versus AOT; README numbers from an older, since-rewritten harness; CPU and compiler unstated; vector sin/cos/log10 use lower-precision Highway approximations.
